item.title: Bomb-thrower Dem makes shocking promise to kick Schumer to curb during Senate debate
item.description: Seth Moulton vowed not to support Chuck Schumer as Senate leader, intensifying a Democratic Party clash between younger candidates and establishment.
item.content:encoded:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., could be facing headwinds in his quest for power even if Democrats win back Congress' upper chamber in November.

Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., who is running in a heated primary against incumbent Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., said during a debate Monday night that he would not support Schumer as leader if elected.

"The first vote that I take when I get to the United States Senate will be for not Senator Schumer, because we need new leadership at the top as well," Moulton said.

MASSACHUSETTS SENATE CANDIDATES TRADE SHARP ATTACKS IN FIERY DEBATE AS INCUMBENT MARKEY SKIPS EVENT

He was alluding to the selection of each party's leadership ranks, which generally comes after the November election.

Markey also did not explicitly endorse Schumer for leader, but he has supported him in the past. Markey’s campaign directed Fox News Digital to the senator’s comments during the debate when asked about his support for Schumer.

"We need a big debate about new leadership in the Senate – the direction of the Senate," Markey said.

It's a notable move for both Democrats to distance themselves from the current party leader, as the primary for Massachusetts' Senate seat has been marked by bitter accusations on both sides.

Moulton has accused Markey of selling out his beliefs by taking money from fossil fuel groups, and slammed the 80-year-old senator for his age and lengthy tenure in Congress. Meanwhile, Markey has attacked Moulton for investing in defense companies that the House committees he sits on have jurisdiction over, and his prior comments on transgender participation in youth sports.

The Salem-area House Democrat has a notable history of challenging his party's leadership. In 2018, he led a rebellion within his caucus to challenge former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., from keeping her leadership post.

He said in a 2019 HuffPost interview that Democratic leadership was "failing" in standing up to President Donald Trump and accused leaders of fueling divisions within the caucus.

Now that fight is playing out in deep blue Massachusetts as part of a wider national war within the Democratic Party. Younger candidates are challenging the establishment left in races across the U.S., arguing that the status quo is not working for Americans today.

HOUSE PROGRESSIVES REVIVE GREEN NEW DEAL FOR PUBLIC SCHOOLS AS DEM CIVIL WAR EMPOWERS FAR LEFT

"If you think the Democratic establishment is winning for Massachusetts, if you think it's fine that the Democratic establishment has allowed a second term of Donald Trump, then vote for the status quo," Moulton said during the debate.

Schumer is not up for re-election until 2028, but he must face his fellow Senate Democrats every two years in the internal leadership race to make a case for why he should stay at the helm.

And younger candidates like Moulton could pose issues for him on that front.

Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., who at 53 years old is younger than a significant number of his colleagues, was evasive when asked if Schumer should remain in leadership during an interview on CNN's "State of the Union" in March.

SCHUMER DODGES QUESTION ON WHETHER DSA BELONGS IN DEMOCRATIC PARTY

"Well, I think we are united right now as a caucus. There’s always a lot of focus on Senator Schumer and [House Minority] Leader Jeffries," Murphy said when asked if he supported Schumer, who he said had a "tough job."

Abdul El-Sayed, a Democratic socialist running in the Michigan Senate primary against an opponent backed by the New York Democrat, said at a recent rally, "If you're Chuck Schumer, I'm pretty damn dangerous."

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

And Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., has also called on Schumer to step aside and make way for new leadership.

Fox News Digital reached out to Schumer's office and Markey's campaign for comment on Moulton's remarks.

item.title: Ted Cruz urges Senate to stay in Washington until Protect College Sports Act passes this week
item.description: President Donald Trump says he's hopeful for a Senate floor vote on the "Protect College Sports Act," but political hurdles could push action into September.
item.content:encoded:
After the Big Ten and SEC agreed to throw their support behind the "Protect College Sports Act" during an intense negotiating period last week, congressional leaders have finally released final text language around the legislation.

On Monday, while meeting with reporters in the Oval Office, President Donald Trump mentioned that he was hopeful that a vote would finally take place on the Senate floor regarding the legislation that has led to plenty of contentious moments behind the scenes.

The bipartisan bill, which was first introduced by Senators Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., along with Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., has been the talk of college athletics over the past week, which comes on the heels of a strenuous stretch of negotiations.

LAWMAKERS PRAISE BIPARTISAN EFFORTS LED BY TRUMP ADMIN TO ‘PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS FOR FUTURE GENERATIONS’

While other conferences across the country had put their support behind the legislation that had yet to be finalized, the SEC and Big Ten wanted to see concessions made that would garner their approval.

After pushing for their support and pointing toward this week as when the legislation could be voted on, having this move into the month of September could end up generating a lane in which this might not be passed at all, with congressional leaders focused on midterms and other important matters for the country.

RUNNING OUT OF TIME: SEC, BIG TEN WAIT ON 'PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT' REVISIONS AS AUGUST RECESS NEARS

That is obviously not in the best interest of those involved in this process, given the amount of work that has gone into putting this bill together.

Last Friday, after a nudge from the White House, senators finally received the support of the two biggest conferences in college sports. But even then, those involved had not seen a final bill, rather given a walkthrough from those involved around Capitol Hill.

The night before, sources told OutKick/Fox News Digital that White House officials, along with members of Trump's college sports committee, were involved in conversations on what the next steps would be to get this to the Senate floor.

TICK TOCK: SEC AND BIG TEN RECEIVE REVISED PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT AS SENATE VOTE TIMELINE LOOMS

Right now, one of the more interesting discussion points between parties involved is when this could actually be voted on. Given that final language had not been presented as of Monday afternoon, Senate Majority Leader John Thune had still not started the cloture process.

By the close of business on Monday night, and early Tuesday morning, Thune did not start the cloture procedure, and the likelihood of this getting to a vote by Friday dwindles by the day for this week.

On a call with a group of reporters Monday afternoon, a Senate Commerce Committee aide mentioned that there were political hurdles in getting this to a vote before Congress takes their August recess later in the week.

Some of those other priorities for the Senate included Russia sanctions, confirmation of nominations and the CLARITY Act among others.

But, Cruz was still persistent in his message that the Senate should stay in Washington until this was passed. There are also other issues that should certainly take precedent over a college sports bill, like the ongoing fires in Spokane, where Cantwell was rightfully attending to over the weekend.

According to language in the bill, which could still be tweaked, obtained by Fox News Digital/OutKick, there were a number of changes made compared to the first version.

Among them are final amendments to the pooling of media rights, how many schools each conference is allowed to have and a retention pool that is separate from the House settlement pool that was established last year.

Schools using a Multimedia Rights partner to push funds towards an athlete, which would be a way for a school to circumvent the revenue-share cap.

A retention pool, separate from House settlement, that will allow schools to use $22.5 million for retaining players. An additional $5 million for women’s/olympic sports.

Conferences cannot exceed 19 member institutions. No, a school cannot skirt the rule

The 'Lane Kiffin Rule' is still in the bill, but it now comes with a punch.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

This provision to the bill will obviously be challenged.. The 'Lane Kiffin Rule' would also affect the school looking to make a change midseason, and start the process of finding a replacement.

An athletic department is not going to wait around until after the season ends to announce/or hire their new coach. And, if this were to be brought before a court, a coach would have a good argument that the government is hindering their ability to obtain work.

As for what is next, that depends on how quick this can be brought for cloture.

A number of sources have mentioned that getting this voted on by Friday evening will be a tall task. But, that doesn’t mean Senators are not going to try.

Given the amount of rebuttal this could receive from Senators who are not in favor of the 'Protect College Sports Act', like Sen. Tommy Tuberville and others, this process could drag into September when Congress returns from recess.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Getting this to a vote this week is going to be tough. Presenting this to Senate leaders in September could present more of a path for passage, and even that part is up in the air.

Stay tuned, because the conversation around "saving college sports" has just begun.

item.title: Ceuta migrant surge exposes Spain-Morocco tensions as Islamist groups reportedly seek to exploit border crisis
item.description: Spain reports 72 deaths as the Ceuta migrant crisis deepens, with intelligence officials saying Morocco allowed border controls to gradually relax.
item.content:encoded:
Thousands of migrants remained stranded in Spain’s North African city of Ceuta on Tuesday as the European Union offered emergency assistance to reinforce the enclave’s border and Spanish authorities investigated whether criminals or suspected jihadists used last week’s chaotic mass crossing to enter European territory.

Approximately 72,000 people entered Ceuta from Morocco, and about 70,000 have since returned, Spanish officials said Tuesday, leaving roughly 2,000 people in the small territory. Reception facilities remained overwhelmed as authorities struggled to shelter hundreds of migrant minors and determine the status of those who remained.

Local authorities were processing 862 migrant minors, who receive special protections under Spanish law and cannot be summarily returned. The Associated Press reported that children were begging for food or sleeping outside after the youth shelter became overwhelmed.

SPAIN DEPLOYS MILITARY AFTER THOUSANDS OF MIGRANTS OVERWHELM BORDER ENCLAVE, AT LEAST 18 DEAD

The EU offered Spain assistance, including emergency financial support, to strengthen protection of its external border in Ceuta, European Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner said Tuesday following an emergency meeting of the bloc’s ministers in Brussels.

Brunner said the unprecedented crossing was fueled by criminal smuggling networks and disinformation spread through social media, as Spanish authorities were examining whether known criminals or suspected jihadists exploited the scale and disorder of the crossing to enter Ceuta undetected.

Spain’s National Police and Guardia Civil were reviewing video of the crossings and checking people who remained in the territory against criminal and counterterrorism databases, according to El Confidencial, which cited Spanish Interior Ministry sources.

The Spanish outlet reported that authorities were searching for known criminals and possible jihadists who may have entered among the tens of thousands who crossed. Interior Ministry sources acknowledged that the sheer scale of the surge created a genuine infiltration risk, according to the report.

El Confidencial said the concern was heightened by Ceuta’s proximity to Fnideq, also known as Castillejos, a Moroccan border town that has figured in previous jihadist recruitment investigations. Authorities have previously dismantled extremist cells operating across the Ceuta-Fnideq border area, while hundreds of people from northern Morocco traveled to join ISIS and other terrorist groups in Syria and Iraq during the mid-2010s, the outlet reported.

TRUMP BLASTS SPAIN MIGRANT SURGE AS 'CATASTROPHE,' WARNS US COULD FACE WORSE IF DEMOCRATS REGAIN POWER

The crisis is also creating an opening for Islamist movements seeking to weaken confidence in Morocco’s government, according to Zineb Riboua, a research fellow at the Hudson Institute.

Riboua said in an article that Moroccan Islamists have spent years portraying the monarchy as overly secular and pro-Western, attacking its relationships with the United States and Israel and encouraging the belief that young Moroccans have little future at home.

At the same time, she wrote, Islamist voices have promoted an idealized image of Europe as a place where prosperity and legal status can be easily obtained.

Riboua said the Ceuta crisis allows those movements to transform public frustration over migration, unemployment and economic conditions into a broader political attack on the Moroccan state ahead of the national elections in September.

Evidence has separately emerged that the mass crossing was preceded by an extensive online mobilization campaign.

An open-source intelligence report prepared by Golden Owl Intelligence traced weeks of activity across TikTok, Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, including misleading interpretations of Spanish immigration law and practical information about routes, meeting points and recommended crossing times.

The report estimated that the content generated more than 11 million potential impressions through posts, videos, comments and interactions. It also identified messaging groups administered through telephone numbers carrying Algerian international codes.

The campaign accelerated after Spain’s Supreme Court issued a July 8 ruling concerning the immediate return of migrants intercepted at sea near Ceuta and Melilla, according to the report. Simplified and misleading interpretations of the decision, combined with confusion surrounding Spain’s policy to regularize hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrants, were presented online as evidence that people who reached Spanish territory would be allowed to remain and eventually obtain legal status.

The investigation documented the later circulation of maps, swimming routes, transportation information and suggested departure points as tens of thousands of people began moving toward the border.

MIGRANT CRISIS PUSHES ITALY TO RESTORE BORDER CHECKS WITH SPAIN, TESTING EUROPE'S OPEN-BORDER SYSTEM

Morocco’s Interior Ministry spokesman Rachid El Khalfi said at a news conference Sunday that the surge resulted from several overlapping factors, including the exploitation of digital platforms, misleading information, human-trafficking networks and inaccurate interpretations of legal and administrative developments.

Khalfi said the messaging created the false impression that the border was open and that people could reach European territory without legal consequences. He said Moroccan prosecutors had opened investigations to identify those responsible and determine the appropriate legal consequences.

Reuters and the Associated Press have independently documented cases in which online claims influenced people to travel toward Ceuta. Reuters interviewed a Moroccan teenager who said Instagram videos inspired him and his cousin to make the journey, while a Moroccan human-rights activist told the AP that social-media posts initially claimed the border was open and later promoted a misleading interpretation of the Supreme Court ruling.

The crisis has also placed Spain’s intelligence services and its relationship with Morocco under scrutiny.

El País and Cadena SER reported, citing officials familiar with Spain’s intelligence assessment, that Morocco did not plan the mass crossing but allowed it to unfold after border controls were gradually relaxed.

Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said Spain’s foreign intelligence agency had not warned him of an imminent surge of that magnitude.

WHITE HOUSE BLASTS SPANISH GOVERNMENT AS THOUSANDS OF MIGRANTS SURGE FROM MOROCCO, EMERGENCY REQUEST DENIED

Morocco has denied deliberately orchestrating the crossing. Interior Ministry spokesman Rachid Khalfi blamed the surge on online misinformation, human-trafficking networks and distorted interpretations of Spanish legal and administrative developments, according to The Jerusalem Post. The ministry said Morocco remained committed to international cooperation against irregular migration and human trafficking.

Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares defended Rabat’s response, saying Moroccan authorities quickly provided police support and helped facilitate the return of most of those who crossed.

Juan Jesus Vivas Lara, president of the autonomous city of Ceuta, offered a sharply different assessment, telling El País that many Ceuta residents believed Morocco had allowed, if not orchestrated, the surge.

"Morocco has shown us that it isn’t reliable," Vivas said. "There’s no alternative but to put in place whatever means are necessary to ensure it cannot do this again."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Moroccan government for comment but did not receive a response by the time of publication.

Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: DOJ charges 19 defendants in alleged $4M Philadelphia Medicare and Medicaid fraud
item.description: The Department of Justice expanded its Northeast Health Care Fraud Strike Force to Philadelphia, charging 19 defendants in alleged Medicare and Medicaid schemes.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: The Justice Department announced Tuesday that it is expanding its Northeast Health Care Fraud Strike Force to Philadelphia as federal and state authorities target alleged Medicare and Medicaid fraud involving home health care services.

The expansion will establish a strike force office in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania and bring together the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the district.

In connection with the announcement, federal and Pennsylvania authorities charged 19 defendants accused of participating in schemes involving more than $4 million in claims submitted to Medicare and Medicaid, according to a DOJ release obtained by Fox News. The defendants include home health care company owners, employees, purported aides and Medicaid recipients.

Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday also announced a plea agreement involving the final defendant in a previously charged 21-defendant case tied to more than $1.7 million in claims.

LETITIA JAMES HAMMERED AFTER NY MEDICAID FRAUD UNIT FUNDING FROZEN OVER INEFFECTIVE ENFORCEMENT

"The Fraud Division’s expansion into the Eastern District of Pennsylvania brings enhanced federal resources to a district with an established tradition of strong health care fraud enforcement," the DOJ said. "The partnership between the Fraud Division and the Eastern District of Pennsylvania will uniquely enable law enforcement to combat criminals who hide behind corporations to commit fraud."

The cases include allegations that home health aides billed Medicaid for services while they were incarcerated, hospitalized, working other jobs or traveling overseas. In another case, prosecutors said a Medicaid recipient claimed to require extensive home health assistance while also working as a carpenter.

Other defendants allegedly submitted overlapping or impossible work hours, including claims exceeding 24 hours of care in a single day, according to the release. One home health care agency and its owners were also charged with allegedly billing Medicaid for false clock-ins and clock-outs.

DOJ CHARGES 10 SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA DEFENDANTS IN LARGEST FEDERAL HEALTHCARE FRAUD CRACKDOWN IN US HISTORY

"The Strike Force’s expansion makes clear that the Fraud Division will use every available legal tool to identify, investigate, and prosecute offenses against the American people," the DOJ said.

The Philadelphia office will work with the Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General, the FBI, the DEA and other law enforcement agencies.

The DOJ said the expansion follows recent additions to the strike force program in California, Arizona, Nevada, Massachusetts and Minnesota, as well as two national health care fraud enforcement actions involving more than $15 billion in alleged losses in 2025 and more than $6 billion in alleged losses in 2026.

item.title: NBA great says he nearly 'dropped dead' due to blood clot as he offers advice to Victor Wembanyama
item.description: Chris Bosh warns Victor Wembanyama about deep vein thrombosis after his own near-death pulmonary embolism forced him into early NBA retirement.
item.content:encoded:
Chris Bosh wants to spread awareness of blood clots after he nearly "dropped dead" earlier this year.

Back in February, Bosh, who was forced to retire because of his history of blood clots, said that he woke up "covered" in his own blood. He recently revealed that he suffered from a pulmonary embolism.

A pulmonary embolism normally occurs when a blood clot breaks loose and travels to the lungs.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

"I almost dropped dead pretty much and came back to life. I'm not joking," Bosh told Hoops Hype.

"I was in the hospital for a week. But, take your medicine. So, I'm taking my medicine every day, taking care of myself every day, and watching it. So, I mean, no symptoms came either, you know, so. Yeah, you got to deal with it for the rest of your life. I thought I was past it. I am not. So, you know, it's just making sure I stay on top of my regimen."

Bosh also offered advice to Victor Wembanyama, who suffered a blood clot that ended his second NBA season in 2024-25.

"Take your medicine," Bosh said. "Make sure that he's staying on top of his regimen to make sure that doesn't happen again, because it only takes one more time. It happened one more time for me, it happened twice, and I couldn't play anymore. So I guess with him, just making sure he does everything necessary to keep that blood as thin as possible and take care of that body off the court."

Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is a condition in which blood clots form in one or more of the deep veins in the body, according to the Mayo Clinic. The condition typically affects the legs and can cause swelling and pain.

TERRY ROZIER'S ATTORNEY SEEKS DISMISSAL CITING TEXT FROM CO-DEFENDANT THAT SHOULD 'END THE CASE': REPORTS

In 2015, Bosh was hospitalized after developing a blood clot in his lung. He had initially ignored the pain in his chest, believing it was just a rib injury. Tests proved otherwise.

Then, in 2016, blood clots continued to form for Bosh, which caused him to fail his physicals with the Miami Heat, with whom he spent six of his 13 NBA seasons. He eventually retired officially from the league in 2017.

Damian Lillard also suffered a blood clot in his right calf last year and missed roughly a month before tearing his left Achilles tendon in the playoffs. He did, however, take part in, and win, the 3-point contest after re-signing with the Portland Trail Blazers.

Wembanyama recently signed a five-year, $252 million, maximum rookie contract extension with the San Antonio Spurs after the Spurs lost the NBA Finals to the New York Knicks.

Fox News' Scott Thompson contributed to this report.

item.title: Socialist Francesca Hong struggles to explain call to 'Cancel Thanksgiving' as post resurfaces
item.description: Francesca Hong fielded questions about a deleted 2020 post calling to cancel Thanksgiving over colonialism and the pandemic during a CNN appearance.
item.content:encoded:
Francesca Hong, the outspoken democratic socialist leading in the polls for the party’s nomination for Wisconsin governor, is making waves for comments she made about an annual American tradition during an interview with CNN on Monday.

While appearing on "The Source with Kaitlan Collins," Hong fielded questions from Collins regarding a previous social media post she made in which she suggested that Americans should cancel their celebrations of the Thanksgiving holiday.

"Do you still believe that Thanksgiving should be canceled?" Collins asked.

SOCIALIST FRONTRUNNER IN THE HOT SEAT AFTER 'CANCEL THANKSGIVING' POST EMERGES ONLINE

"I’m a chef, and one of the first meals that I made that was for the community when I was 16 [years old] was a Thanksgiving meal," Hong said. "I always think my hospitality background in owning a restaurant for seven, eight years, that bringing folks around the table to share conversation and build community is always a good thing."

Hong, a 37-year-old state assemblywoman hailing from Madison, then seemed to double down on her condemnation of the annual American tradition.

"But Thanksgiving is also a time that’s incredibly painful for many people in our communities," Hong continued. "And so I think there, I wanted to make sure that people understood that there are multiple views, but views can evolve."

"And the position that I'm running for right now, and I think my background as a chef will actually help me become a better governor that's able to bring more people to the table," she concluded.

WISCONSIN DEM SOCIALIST GUBERNATORIAL HOPEFUL DODGES WHETHER SHE STILL WANTS TO ‘ABOLISH POLICE’

The now-deleted post, which was initially made on X in November 2020, drew backlash after Hong appeared to draw comparisons between the deadly pandemic and the Thanksgiving holiday.

"Cancel Thanksgiving. Should have done this in 1621," Hong wrote, according to Fox News Digital’s previous reporting.

"If it takes a worldwide pandemic for us to realize we should stop celebrating colonialism and the original superspreader event that killed indigenous folx [sic] and women, so be it," she added, referring to the spread of smallpox that killed many indigenous Americans.

The term "folx" is reportedly used to signal inclusivity of LGBTQ+ and other marginalized groups.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Hong's campaign said, "No, she does not want to 'cancel' Thanksgiving."

PROGRESSIVE MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE'S STAFFER RAGED AT WHITE WOMEN IN UNEARTHED POSTS

CHUCK TODD SUGGESTS DNC PRIMARY CALENDAR INTENDED TO THWART POTENTIAL PROGRESSIVE INSURGENT CANDIDATE IN 2028

Hong's answer drew mockery from conservatives on X.

"[W]ord salad that would make Kamala [Harris] envious," Libs of TikTok wrote.

The post is not the only instance of Hong taking to social media to share her polarizing views. In a resurfaced 2019 post, Hong posted about being "on the verge of [an] anxiety attack" while dining at a popular fast food restaurant with her son.

Hong, who is endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America, is leading in the Democratic primary race ahead of next week's election.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

She has received the support of several progressives on the national stage, including Hasan Piker, Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., and shares similar policy positions with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Fox News Digital’s Leo Briceno contributed to this report.

item.title: Left’s latest socialist darling dragged over ‘whiteness’ comments pulling in her own family: ‘Weirdo racism’

"My proximity to whiteness continues, right... My son is biracial. He is half-white and half-Korean. I think navigating what his identity is and how people perceive him is always at the back of my mind as well," Hong, who has served in the Wisconsin State Assembly since 2021, said during a 2021 interview with ListenMKE.

A trove of Hong's past X posts and interview clips has resurfaced as she campaigns for Wisconsin governor, renewing scrutiny of her repeated comments about race and identity, including remarks critical of whiteness.

HASAN PIKER'S DEFENSE OF HAMAS HAVING 'RIGHT TO RESIST MILITARILY' DRAWS CONDEMNATION FROM HUMAN RIGHTS GROUPS

"2018- old white dude asks ‘where are you from?’ 2019- old white dude asks ‘what is your country of origin’ My ramen bar has become a customs kiosk," Hong wrote in another post in May of the same year.

item.title: Top media outlets fail to disclose who is bankrolling their AI reporters
item.description: Major outlets like Time and The Verge aren't disclosing that their AI reporters are funded by a nonprofit backed by an Anthropic investor.
item.content:encoded:
Several major news organizations are hosting reporter fellows with salaries paid by donor-supported AI journalism groups — relationships that frequently go undisclosed.

The Tarbell Center for AI Journalism places fellows with outlets like Bloomberg, Time, NBC News, The Guardian and the Los Angeles Times. And while some outlets are alerting readers to those funding relationships, others aren’t, raising questions about how disclosure standards are applied.

The Tarbell Center for AI Journalism pays its fellows between $60,000 and $80,000, and fellows with at least five years of experience can make between $90,000 and $110,000.

AI CHATBOTS TAKE HEAT OVER LEFT-WING BIAS: ‘NO LONGER BE CONSIDERED NEUTRAL’

"Tarbell is committed to supporting independent journalism that demystifies the debates around this technology, holds the companies and people building it to account and fosters the discourse necessary to chart a path that benefits society," the group states on its website.

Tarbell has sponsored at least 28 journalists covering topics like Anthropic, deepfakes, AI in geopolitics, misuse, the economy and misinformation. On its website, the group states that it does not set the direction of its reporters’ work.

"Our donors have no editorial control over the work of Tarbell, our fellows, or our grantees. Tarbell does not accept anonymous donations greater than $10,000," the website says.

The group also emphasized the policy in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"All our fellows maintain strict editorial independence. Tarbell does not dictate the conclusions or perspectives of the journalists we support — their reporting is guided only by facts they uncover, not predetermined narratives. This is outlined in our editorial independence policies, which are strongly emphasized throughout the process of recruiting, vetting, and training the fellows," Cillian Crosson, executive director of the Tarbell Center, said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

Even so, Tarbell says it receives funding from Coefficient Giving, the Future of Life Institute, the EA Infrastructure Fund and the Survival and Flourishing Fund — all groups that advocate for their ideals on AI safety. Coefficient Giving, in particular, has awarded more than $4.7 million to Tarbell, according to the organization's public grants' database.

More pointedly still, Coefficient Giving is backed primarily by Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz, an Anthropic investor.

In the case of Anthropic, many of Tarbell’s fellows have written material covering the company.

Harry Booth, a reporter working with Time, wrote an article titled "The War for AI," calling Claude, Anthropic’s flagship AI, a "world-class model" after visiting the company’s California headquarters. Time did not disclose Booth’s support from Tarbell in his story.

ABC NEWS FACES BACKLASH FOR PRESENTING OBAMA CAMPAIGN AD AS AN 'EXCLUSIVE' ON REDISTRICTING MEASURE

Similarly, The Verge did not mention reporter Robert Hart’s paid fellowship as he authored an article on OpenAI, the parent company of ChatGPT, when he covered the Trump administration’s clash with Anthropic over security concerns.

Time said disclosure decisions are left to its editors.

"TIME is committed to transparency. Current Tarbell Fellows’ affiliations are disclosed in their TIME author biographies. TIME’s editorial decisions are determined solely by our editors," the outlet said in a statement.

The Verge did not respond to requests for comment.

Notably, some outlets have chosen to outline connections to Tarbell at the bottom of their stories. NBC News added an editorial note to the work of Jared Perlo, a fellow who reports on the Future of Life Institute, a group that evaluates AI safety.

"This reporter is a Tarbell Fellow, funded through the Tarbell Center for AI Journalism, a nonprofit devoted to supporting the news coverage of artificial intelligence," NBC wrote at the bottom of the report.

OPENAI'S SAM ALTMAN WANTS TO NEGOTIATE A 5% STAKE IN COMPANY FOR US IF COMPETITORS AGREE TO KEY PROVISION

item.title: Texans' Jalen Pitre named first-ever NFL Guardian Cap athlete in league history: 'Evolution of the game'
item.description: Jalen Pitre explains why he became the first-ever NFL Guardian athlete and predicts the protective cap will soon become football's new norm.
item.content:encoded:
The National Football League made a major move toward player safety in 2020 when Guardian Caps were introduced. Just two years later, they were made mandatory for select positions in practices.

But history is changing once again, as Houston Texans safety Jalen Pitre has been named the first-ever NFL Guardian athlete.

"I think the biggest thing is just spreading the message that football is important to me, and it needs to be played the right way with the right things. Guardian Cap is the league and NCAA sponsor, and it is the right way to protect yourself," Pitre told Fox News Digital in a recent interview. "I believe that I should be wearing them and that others should be wearing them as well. I also want to spread the message to the kids who don’t get to see our practices, where we wear them regularly."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Pitre's decision was an easy one as he continued to wear the cap, which is now mandatory in padded practices for everyone but quarterbacks. As a safety, he gets down-and-dirty often, and he felt a difference right away.

"They want to protect us, so everyone can make it to the game healthy. I want to make it home healthy as well, so why not take an extra step and wear it in the game as well? Having a cap on allows your head to absorb hits better and makes the hits on top of your head a lot softer," Pitre said.

49ERS STAR WIDE RECEIVER RICKY PEARSALL OUT FOR THE SEASON, TO UNDERGO SURGERY ON KNEE IN CRUSHING BLOW

It's not common for now, but Pitre believes that the Guardian Cap can, and will, become a mainstay.

"I see it as an evolution of the game. I feel like Guardian Cap is going to be congruent with football eventually and integrated into how they make helmets. It will be the new norm, and when my kids play football, they will all have Guardian Caps, and nobody will think anything of it," he said.

"Even if you look at the helmets they used to make compared to the helmets now, it’s a complete change."

Pitre knows that it's difficult to convince others to wear the cap, as it's not exactly the most stylish-looking piece of clothing. 

"If I’m making plays and doing well in it," Pitre, fresh off a career-high four interceptions, said, "it looks cool, and it will be easier for others to follow."

item.title: Trade vessel struck by projectile in Strait of Hormuz amid US-Iran talks
item.description: A trade vessel reported being struck by an unknown projectile near Oman's coast as Trump claims a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz is imminent.
item.content:encoded:
A trade vessel in the Strait of Hormuz reported being struck by a projectile overnight Tuesday as it was transiting near the coast of Oman.

The incident, reported to U.K. Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), comes amid conflicting reports of Iran participating in peace talks with the U.S. this week. President Donald Trump said on Monday that a deal to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz and denuclearize Iran was "imminent."

The UKMTO offered few details about the incident, saying only that the vessel had been struck "by an unknown projectile" at roughly 2 a.m. local time while it was 23 miles northeast of Al Khasab in Oman. The UKMTO did not clarify the name of the vessel or what flag it was flying under, nor did it note any injuries from the incident.

The British maritime security firm Ambrey confirmed the ship suffered damage but did not elaborate.

US CLAWS BACK KEY CONCESSION TO IRAN AFTER FRESH ATTACKS ON COMMERCIAL SHIPS IN STRAIT OF HORMUZ

The incident comes as Iran has denied engaging in talks with the U.S., despite statements from multiple parties that talks are indeed ongoing.

Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari said Tuesday said all parties were engaged in mediation and are "looking into a diplomatic solution."

A spokesman for Iran's foreign ministry denied talks with the U.S. on Monday, saying Tehran was only involved in negotiations with Oman regarding the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump acknowledged the mixed messages with frustration in a number of statements on Monday, insisting that Tehran officials were engaged in talks with the U.S. regardless of what they were saying publicly.

TRUMP WARNS IRAN FIGHTING ISN'T OVER AS HE VOWS US WILL 'WIN' AS TALKS FADE

"They ask for a meeting, some would say ‘beg,’ talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they’re not having any discussions, that nothing is being talked about, and they’re only dealing with ‘Oman’," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.

"For some reason they, when they're talking, they don't like saying that they're talking," Trump said later during an Oval Office event. "So I say we're in talks, big deal, we're in talks. And they'll sometimes deny it even though they spend hours and hours together talking."

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Bad bosses on Capitol Hill could face reckoning under new anonymous staffer review platform
item.description: Capitol CNCT lets verified congressional staffers anonymously rate and review their offices, revealing early rankings of the best and worst bosses.
item.content:encoded:
Capitol Hill staffers typically rely on private conversations and faceless social media accounts to identify toxic offices — but a new platform is offering a verified place to anonymously rate and review members of Congress and the workplaces they run.

Capitol CNCT, a program designed to centralize resources for congressional staffers, launched on July 20 a new tool called "The Scoop," where verified staffers can share anonymous, but verified, reviews of the offices where they're employed.

Former staffer David Tennent told Fox News Digital he founded Capitol CNCT to modernize the experience for young people working in congressional offices in Washington, D.C. He said the idea of the new ranking system emerged due to growing frustration over the number of "bad bosses" and "toxic offices" in the halls of Congress.

CAPITOL HILL SEX SCANDALS TRIGGER NEW PUSH TO REDRAW THE LINE FOR LAWMAKERS

"I wanted to create something that gave a little bit more transparency to the process and help staffers find the best opportunities available," he said in an interview detailing his inspiration for the new tool.

Just a week after launch, verified reviews are already beginning to paint an early picture of workplace culture across Capitol Hill.

While most offices still have only a handful of ratings, the highest-rated House offices so far are Reps. Nick LaLota, R-N.Y., Abe Hamadeh, R-Ariz., Brendan Boyle, D-Pa., Michael Rulli, R-Ohio, and Robert Garcia, D-Calif.

Among Senate offices, the top five were Sens. Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala., Todd Young, R-Ind., Thom Tillis, R-N.C., Eric Schmitt, R-Miss., and Kevin Cramer, R-N.D.

Across both chambers, the five lowest-rated offices were Rep. Don Davis, D-N.C., Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill., Rep. Julia Brownley, D-Calif., Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., and Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo.

The offices of Davis, Krishnamoorthi, Brownley, Van Hollen and Bennet did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on their rankings.

ANGER SWELLS AFTER SWALWELL'S 'OPEN SECRET' WITH WOMEN WENT UNREPORTED FOR YEARS

There is no centralized human resources department for members’ offices on the Hill — making it tricky for staffers to report toxic or abusive workplaces.

"The Scoop" aims to offer a reliable place where people can leave and review feedback from staff who have gone through a verification process, which ensures anyone leaving a review actually works in the office they are rating.

"We verify the office in which they've worked," Tennent told Fox News Digital. "We sift through all reviews before they go live to our platform to make sure that staffer has actually worked in that office."

Reviews are only published if the user leaving feedback passes Capitol CNCT’s background screening to ensure they have at some point worked for the member of Congress they are commenting on. The process includes verifying House and Senate email addresses attached to the account are legitimate.

"My biggest fear was just creating like a political retribution platform, right?" Tennent explained. "Where you can just go on and destroy people without any evidence or verification that you've been a part of that process."

Tennent revealed that Republican offices are almost twice as likely to be reviewed than Democrats’ offices so far.

The launch last month comes amid heightened scrutiny of workplace culture on Capitol Hill after multiple offices faced misconduct allegations this year.

REPUBLICAN LAWMAKER WELCOMES HOUSE ETHICS PROBE INTO SEXUAL MISCONDUCT ALLEGATIONS AGAINST HIM

Many members of Congress have either resigned or been under fire this year for allegations of inappropriate behavior with members of their staff.

Rep. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., and Rep. Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, both resigned in April after staffers from their offices came forward with accusations of sexual misconduct — including rape accusations against Swalwell.

"We happened to be able to launch it right in this timeframe where this congressional ethics or lack of morality discussion is really hitting its high pitch," Tennent said.

Tennent said that while the main purpose of the app is to give staffers, or those considering working on the Hill, verifiable reviews about what it is like working for certain members of Congress, he also hopes it will serve as constructive criticism for members and their offices "to create a better working Congress."

"We do want to provide like constructive criticism in this process," Tennent said

He continued, "Our hope is that if a chief of staff or a member sees that their office is very poorly rated, that over time they're gonna go, ‘Oh, this is a wake-up call for me. Let me implement some strategies to boost office morale, to change how we communicate with each other.’"

item.title: New '60 Minutes' producer hopes to crack down on 'rumors' leaked to press following dramatic shakeup
item.description: Nick Bilton's staff memo pushes back on daily newsroom drama leaks, calling 95% of rumors about the "60 Minutes" overhaul blatantly incorrect.
item.content:encoded:
Newly minted "60 Minutes" executive producer Nick Bilton is hoping to tamp down the leaks to the press about newsroom drama, much of which he insists are false.

"Since I started here there has been roughly a rumor a day. About me, about you, about what's coming next — 95% percent of them are fabrications and blatantly incorrect," Bilton wrote Monday in a staff memo obtained by Fox News Digital. "I no longer have the time or the patience for them, and I'd rather we spend that energy on the stories."

"If you hear something and it matters to you, come ask me and I'll tell you what I know. Otherwise, I'd like this place to be talked about for what we put on television," he added.

FIRED ‘60 MINUTES’ CORRESPONDENTS SHARYN ALFONSI AND SCOTT PELLEY WASH UP AT COLUMBIA JOURNALISM SCHOOL

Bilton spent much of the memo, which was first reported by Status News, going over "housekeeping notes" ahead of the show's 59th season set to air next month, including where his new office is, planned lunches in the coming weeks and the roll-out of a digital version of the "60 Minutes" story board.

"The story board has been replaced with a digital version that updates in real time with what correspondents, producers and editors are working on. There is no reason in 2026 we should be tracking the #1 show in news using a dry erase marker," Bilton told staff.

FIRED '60 MINUTES' CORRESPONDENT ACCUSES CBS NEWS LEADERSHIP OF MEDDLING IN REPORTING

He also addressed questions staffers have asked him about working in the office, writing, "I firmly believe we're all grownups and I'm not going to take attendance. You're reporting, you're shooting, you're traveling. But this show has never been made by people working alone at desks in different zip codes. When you're not in the field, I'd appreciate it if you can be in the office."

CBS News did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Bilton was handpicked by CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss to lead "60 Minutes" as part of a major overhaul of the longtime magazine program. 

As he was being hired, his predecessor, Tanya Simon, and "60 Minutes" correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega were fired.

CBS ANCHOR DEFENDS LEADERSHIP AMID '60 MINUTES' FALLOUT, 'NOT THE EXPERIENCE THAT I'VE HAD'

Veteran "60 Minutes" correspondent Scott Pelley was also ousted after he lashed out at Bilton and Weiss during Bilton's first meeting with the show's staff.

Last week, Bilton announced that New York Times columnist Ross Douthat and CBS News veteran Norah O'Donnell would join as "60 Minutes" correspondents in addition to a slew of contributors including journalist and documentary filmmaker Sebastian Junger, former Vice News correspondent Gianna Toboni, who was previously tapped by CBS News as a national correspondent, and former Sky News presenter Trevor Phillips, whom CBS News recently hired as its senior global affairs correspondent.

item.title: Oklahoma Sooners quarterback John Mateer looks absolutely jacked just in time for fall camp
item.description: A photo of Oklahoma Sooners quarterback John Mateer shows a stunning physical transformation heading into fall camp for the 2026 college football season.
item.content:encoded:
As we inch ever closer to the start of college football season, many programs are transitioning from player-led workouts straight into fall camp this week.

With that comes position battles, practice reports, and eternal optimism among fans that this is finally "the year."

Some of the most underrated aspects of the start of fall camp, however, are the physical transformations of many of the players on the team from one season to the next.

THREE INTRIGUING QUARTERBACK BATTLES TO WATCH DURING COLLEGE FOOTBALL OFFSEASON CAMPS

August is the first time a good portion of the fanbase has seen some of their favorite players since last season, save for a glorified scrimmage we call a spring game back in April, and with all the work these guys put in over the offseason when it comes to living in the gym and in the cafeteria, the changes can be eye-opening.

One such player who definitely took his offseason strength and conditioning program seriously is Oklahoma Sooners quarterback John Mateer.

Mateer has always been a pretty stoutly built dude, but a picture of the veteran signal caller at the start of Sooners camp is making the rounds on social media and has many people lauding the efforts of new S&C coach James Dobson.

FANS STUNNED AT TRAVIS KELCE'S TRAINING CAMP PHYSIQUE AFTER NUPTIALS TO TAYLOR SWIFT

Good Lord!

What are the feeding these kids in Norman? Mateer is built like he subsisted on a diet of nothing but tomahawk steaks and protein shakes all summer.

He looks like if Tim Tebow ate a slightly skinnier Tim Tebow.

ONE OF THESE EIGHT COLLEGE FOOTBALL TEAMS WILL BE HOISTING THE NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIP TROPHY IN 2026

Mateer suffered a hand injury during the 2025 season that ultimately derailed Oklahoma's goals of winning the SEC.

They still made a College Football Playoff appearance, but their Heisman hopeful quarterback was never the same after the injury.

Reports are that Mateer is fully healthy heading into the start of the 2026 season, and I'd say this picture is all the proof any OU fan needs to confirm that.

Certainly healthy enough to throw around some serious weight in the training facility, that is.

I know the Sooners are supposed to have one of the best defenses in the SEC this season, but if they are short a middle linebacker they could always plug in Mateer in a pinch.

I can hear the haters and doubters saying things like, "having a jacked quarterback doesn't mean Oklahoma will win a national championship," and that's true, at least on its face.

But as I mentioned above, Mateer was a trendy Heisman pick before his hand injury, so bulking up can only stand to help him become more durable.

The Sooners will be a force in both the SEC and national picture, and if the rest of the team took offseason workouts as seriously as Mateer, the rest of the country better watch out.

item.title: Maryland synagogue sues county over law restricting concealed carry near houses of worship
item.description: The Silver Spring Jewish Center claimed Montgomery County's ban on firearms near places of worship violates Second Amendment rights and endangers Jews.
item.content:encoded:
A Maryland synagogue filed a lawsuit against a county law restricting permit holders from carrying weapons within 100 yards of houses of worship in light of rising antisemitic attacks last week.

Montgomery County enacted a law on July 27 that restricted the possession or transport of firearms within 100 yards of "a place of public assembly," which includes a place of worship like a Jewish synagogue. The law provides exceptions for police officers and licensed security guards and does not apply to the possession of firearms in one's private home or the possession of one firearm and ammunition at a place of business by the owner or an authorized employee.

The lawsuit, filed just days later by the New Civil Liberties Alliance (NCLA) on behalf of the Silver Spring Jewish Center and Rabbi J. Menashe Shapiro, accused the county of not only violating Jewish people's constitutional right to bear arms but also endangering them by depriving them of ways to defend themselves.

ORTHODOX JEW ASKS SUPREME COURT TO HEAR CASE AFTER CITY ALLEGEDLY TARGETED HIS HOME PRAYER GROUP

"This ban could not come at a worse time for Montgomery County’s Jewish community. Just a short time after the firebombing in Boulder, the arson attack on Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro’s residence, and — close to home — the shooting at the Capital Jewish Museum, Montgomery County seeks to deprive Jews of their ability to defend themselves at their most Jewish moment: praying in synagogues. Jewish law requires Jews to defend themselves when necessary. Montgomery County would rather declare open season," the lawsuit read.

NCLA also maintained that the recent Supreme Court decision on Wolford v. Lopez, ruling that Hawaii's state law requiring a property owner's explicit permission to allow lawful gun owners to bring firearms into public businesses was unconstitutional, already found that states and municipalities cannot deny citizens their Second Amendment rights.

Shapiro and NCLA Senior Litigation Counsel Jacob Huebert spoke to Fox News Digital about the support they have faced from the Jewish community regarding this lawsuit.

INSIDE TRUMP'S UNPRECEDENTED BATTLE PLAN TO EXPAND SECOND AMENDMENT RIGHTS THROUGH JUSTICE DEPARTMENT

"The Jewish community, not only nationwide, but internationally is behind, is largely supportive of this effort," Shapiro said. "I've received a lot of comments and a lot of feedback from many people. This is, you might say, blown up on Jewish media channels and various sources. People are highly interested. And unfortunately, they perceive the real threat that this bill from Montgomery County poses."

"We've received overwhelmingly positive feedback from this as people recognize how outrageous it is to disarm religious people who face actual credible threats and need to exercise their right to self-defense," Huebert said.

NCLA is demanding that a court rule that the law was in violation of the First, Second and Fourteenth Amendment and permanently enjoin the county from enforcing the law.

Prior to the law, Shapiro explained that the synagogue organized a group of highly-trained licensed volunteers to help protect the area after the Oct. 7 attacks. 

As the lawsuit proceeds, Shapiro said he is focused on protecting his community through legal means.

"I'll say we are doing our best to respond, and we hope that the Maryland courts will very quickly realize what a very dangerous position they put not only any one particular synagogue, but the religious people generally they've exposed to some pretty great risk," Shapiro said.

ORTHODOX JEW FIGHTS BACK, SAYS CALIFORNIA CITY FINED HIM FOR HOME PRAYER MEETINGS

Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon expressed support for the lawsuit on Thursday and warned that the Justice Department would take action if the Maryland county did not block enforcement of the law.

"History teaches us that people are particularly vulnerable to armed attacks during worship. That is why @CivilRights Division @TheJusticeDept is acting quickly to challenge Montgomery Co., MD’s law disarm congregants in houses of worship that permit firearms," Dhillon wrote on X.

Montgomery County initially declined to comment on the lawsuit, telling Fox News Digital that the county "does not comment on pending litigation."

However, Montgomery County Council President Natali Fani-González released a statement defending the law, saying that the restrictions were not a new addition.

"As elected leaders, it’s our responsibility to implement commonsense measures to help safeguard our residents and first responders from the growing epidemic of gun violence. The ban against bringing weapons into places of worship has been in place for decades. This provision wasn’t added in Expedited Bill 23-26, Weapons - Restrictions on Ghost Guns Near Minors and Carrying of Firearms in or Near Places of Public Assembly, which updated Montgomery County’s firearms law to comply with a Maryland Supreme Court decision while preserving the strongest local firearm restrictions authorized under state law," Fani-González told Fox News Digital.

item.title: Cubs star Pete Crow-Armstrong appreciates the wild conspiracy theory that Babe Ruth never existed
item.description: Pete Crow-Armstrong shared his love for the Babe Ruth conspiracy theory on Kristin Cavallari's podcast, citing pitcher Tayler Saucedo's deep dive.
item.content:encoded:
If there is someone in your life who says they don't believe in, or at the very least enjoy, a good conspiracy theory, they are lying to you. There are, of course, different levels of conspiracy theories, and one that involves the idea that one of the greatest baseball players to ever walk the Earth simply didn't exist would be towards the top of the list of crazy.

That isn't stopping Chicago Cubs superstar Pete Crow-Armstrong from being all ears.

During a recent appearance on Kristin Cavallari's 'Let's Be Honest' podcast, PCA was asked to share an unpopular opinion. Instead of answering the basic question with a basic answer – maybe tying it back to food or general life musings – he opted to talk about one of the wildest conspiracies in the sports universe.

PETE CROW-ARMSTRONG LAUNCHES SAVAGE EXTRA-INNING HOME RUN BEFORE CARDINALS GET THE LAST LAUGH

"This is gonna be crazy," Crow-Armstrong began. "Babe Ruth never existed is one that I like...I heard some pitcher with the Mariners, (Tayler) Saucedo, I think he did some podcast on Zoom when he was like going down the rabbit hole about how Babe Ruth never existed, and I was like dude, that's awesome.

"We always talk about how the game is evolving, and people may as well have been underhanding the ball to that guy, and he's regarded still as one of the best players ever. You might as well dive further into it and be like, well maybe he just never existed."

The podcast that Crow-Armstrong referenced does exist, and dates back to a 2024 interview with Saucedo in which he made the claim that Ruth never existed simply because there isn't a lot of footage of him playing.

Ruth played from 1914 to 1935, an era in which cameras and televisions weren't exactly prominent, hence the lack of footage of The Babe on the diamond.

It's worth noting that Crow-Armstrong never definitively said that 'Babe Ruth never existed '; he simply voiced his appreciation for the conspiracy theory given how bizarre it is and that it involves one of the most talked-about athletes in the history of American sports.

Ruth, a first-ballot Hall of Famer, won seven World Series titles and led the American League in home runs 12 times.

Or did he?

item.title: Water cyberattack hits at least 7 states
item.description: CISA warned about exposed programmable logic controllers weeks before hackers targeted dozens of Minnesota water utilities in a coordinated strike.
item.content:encoded:
You probably never think about the computer systems behind your kitchen faucet. You turn the handle and expect clean water. That familiar routine suddenly felt far less certain in Minnesota and six other states.

A coordinated cyberattack targeted operational technology at more than 30 community water systems on Sunday, July 26, and Monday, July 27. Minnesota IT Services, known as MNIT, activated the state's cybersecurity response and brought in federal agencies to help investigate.

One water plant temporarily went offline. Meanwhile, other communities reported problems involving automated controls or communications equipment. Workers switched to manual operations or used backup procedures to keep essential services running. Fortunately, state officials reported no active requests for residents to reduce or change their drinking water use.

The FBI has since said that water or wastewater utility companies in seven states have been affected.

"Some of that activity degraded water operations," the bureau said.

This water cyberattack raises an uncomfortable question for towns across America. How many local utilities could keep operating if hackers gained access to the computers controlling their equipment?

INVESTIGATORS BELIEVE IRANIAN HACKERS ARE LIKELY BEHIND CYBERATTACK ON MINNESOTA WATER SYSTEMS: REPORT

CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?," has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

The attack targeted operational technology, commonly called OT. These systems control physical equipment such as pumps, valves and treatment machinery. In Braham, city officials initially reported that the water plant had gone offline for an unknown reason. Crews restored the facility within hours and said it was again filtering and treating water as expected.

Officials later blamed the outage on a malicious cyberattack against computerized operating systems. The city relied on water already stored in its tower while crews worked on the problem. Plymouth reported communications problems involving two water towers and several wastewater lift stations. However, officials said water levels and water quality remained unaffected.

South St. Paul also identified a cybersecurity incident involving automated water utility controls. Public Works employees used established contingency procedures to maintain normal water and wastewater operations. Maple Plain publicly confirmed that its water utility technology had also been targeted.

In total, four communities have publicly described specific effects, although MNIT says attackers targeted more than 30 systems statewide. That difference is important. Being targeted does not mean every system suffered a shutdown. However, it shows that someone tried to reach a large number of local utilities within a short period.

Officials have not announced a definitive attribution. However, a July 30 report from The New York Times says investigators preliminarily believe Iranian hackers were probably responsible. The report cited U.S. and state officials familiar with the investigation, but President Donald Trump said he rejected the suggestion that Iran was behind the breaches.

Those officials cautioned that the assessment could change as investigators collect more technical evidence. They also have not ruled out the possibility that attackers tried to make the activity appear Iranian. Therefore, Iran should be described as the leading preliminary suspicion rather than the confirmed attacker.

The timing has drawn attention because CISA warned in April that Iranian-affiliated hackers were targeting internet-exposed programmable logic controllers. These devices help control machinery and other equipment at water systems and additional critical infrastructure facilities. CISA initially highlighted certain Rockwell Automation and Allen-Bradley controllers. On July 22, the agency expanded its warning to include equipment from Schneider Electric, Siemens and potentially other manufacturers.

Still, federal officials have not publicly tied that campaign to the Minnesota incidents. CyberGuy has previously examined Iran's expanding cyber threat to U.S. critical infrastructure. Water systems remain attractive targets because even a limited disruption can create fear far beyond the equipment involved.

IRAN-LINKED HACKERS TARGET US MEDICAL TECH COMPANY

Minnesota's experience could happen in any state. The United States has close to 170,000 drinking water and wastewater systems. Many now connect physical equipment to internet-enabled technology so workers can monitor facilities from a distance. That remote access helps utilities manage equipment spread across wide service areas. However, it may also give an attacker a route into vital controls when operators fail to secure the connection.

Smaller communities often face the greatest challenge. The Government Accountability Office says water systems have widely different cybersecurity capabilities. Many also use older technology that can be difficult to update. At the same time, utilities must stretch limited budgets across essential repairs and regulatory requirements. Cybersecurity upgrades may compete with work that residents can see, such as replacing aging equipment.

A large utility may employ dedicated security professionals. A small town may rely on plant operators who already handle daily operations and after-hours problems. As a result, the communities with fewer resources may also have less ability to monitor suspicious activity around the clock.

Foreign governments have already shown interest in those weak spots. CyberGuy previously reported how Chinese hackers gained access to critical American systems, including infrastructure connected to water and energy. The attacker may change. The underlying weakness often looks familiar: exposed equipment, outdated technology or remote access that lacks strong protection.

A cyberattack against a water utility does not automatically mean the water has been contaminated. In Minnesota, officials reported no known impact on drinking water quality. They also told residents in publicly identified communities that normal water use could continue.

However, a successful attack can cause more serious consequences. The EPA warns that hackers could disrupt treatment or damage equipment. In a worst-case situation, attackers might also interfere with processes that protect water quality.

Manual operations can provide an important safety net. Minnesota workers used those procedures to keep systems running while investigators examined affected technology. Still, a manual backup only helps when employees know how to use it. Utilities need to test those procedures before screens go dark and alarms stop reporting correctly.

CISA published new international guidance on July 28 called "CI Fortify: Advice for Isolating Vital Systems." The guidance urges critical infrastructure operators to separate vital operational technology from less trusted networks. That isolation can help an essential service continue operating when another part of the organization becomes compromised.

CISA released the guidance on the same day MNIT publicly announced the statewide attack. However, the agency has not said it created the document in response to Minnesota. For water utilities, stronger protection may begin with removing unnecessary internet exposure. When remote access remains necessary, CISA advises placing security controls in front of programmable controllers.

Utilities should also change factory passwords and give employees separate login credentials. EPA inspectors have found water systems that continued using default passwords. Inspectors also discovered shared staff accounts or access that remained active after employees left.

Another EPA finding needs careful context. The agency says more than 70% of inspected systems violated basic federal risk assessment or emergency response planning requirements. That figure does not mean 70% had confirmed cybersecurity breaches. However, inspectors found serious digital security weaknesses at some of those facilities.

TRUMP REJECTS IRAN BLAME FOR MINNESOTA CYBERATTACK, POINTS FINGER AT 'CORRUPT' POLITICAL FOE

Residents cannot secure a municipal treatment plant themselves. However, a few steps can help you receive reliable information and avoid scams during an incident.

Check your city, county health department or water utility website for updates. Officials will tell you whether you need to reduce water use or boil tap water. Avoid making decisions based on an unverified neighborhood post.

A cyberattack may affect communications or automated equipment without changing water quality. Continue normal use unless local officials provide different instructions. However, follow any boil-water notice immediately if one appears.

Your city may use text messages, automated calls or government phone alerts during a service disruption. Take a moment to check the emergency alert settings on your iPhone or Android. Also, sign up for your city's local notification system if one is available.

A backup supply can help during any water interruption, whether it begins with a cyberattack or equipment failure. The CDC recommends storing at least one gallon of water per person each day for three days. Households may need more for pets or people with medical needs.

Scammers often take advantage of outages and breaking news. You may receive a message claiming that your water bill failed or that your service will be disconnected. Another message may offer bottled water assistance through a payment link. Do not use the phone number or link inside an unexpected message. Instead, contact the utility through its official website or the number printed on your bill. CyberGuy has also explained how scammers impersonate water and other utility companies by spoofing familiar phone numbers.

Minnesota contained a troubling attack without a known drinking water emergency. Workers restored Braham's plant while other utilities relied on manual controls or contingency procedures. However, the number of systems targeted should get the attention of every governor and mayor in America. Hackers apparently found a way to reach dozens of local utilities during the same two-day period. The preliminary suspicion involving Iranian hackers also raises the stakes. Still, investigators need more evidence before anyone treats that attribution as settled. Every community should know which water controls face the internet and whether workers can operate essential equipment manually. States should also help smaller towns that cannot afford their own cybersecurity teams.

How confident are you that your community could handle a cyberattack on its water system, and what would you want local officials to tell you first? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

item.title: Haunting new images reveal the final ship where explorer Sir Ernest Shackleton died
item.description: The first close-up images reveal the remains of Quest in the Labrador Sea, where the historic shipwreck is covered with pink corals, surrounded by marine life and draped in fishing nets.
item.content:encoded:
Officials have released the first close-up images of the remains of Quest, the final ship of the legendary Antarctic explorer Sir Ernest Shackleton.

The images were taken at the ship's location in the Labrador Sea, around 1,280 feet deep in the waters off of Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada, and were released in July. 

After 60 years, the vessel remains recognizable and in moderate condition, Dwight Coleman, co-chief scientist at Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI), told Fox News Digital.

MYSTERY OF GOLD COIN SHIPWRECK FINALLY UNMASKED AFTER 30 YEARS: 'FANTASTIC CONCLUSION'

"You could tell it was a ship," he said. "It had an obvious bow and stern, rudder and propeller.

"Even though it was sort of covered in fishing nets, you could still tell that some of that structure was preserved underneath the nets."

In a statement from the Royal Canadian Geographical Society (RCGS), in partnership with WHOI, officials said the wreck "was populated with pink corals, and several species of fish including cod, red fish and wolf fish."

The images show fishing nets draped across parts of the wreck, as well as parts of its metal superstructure and portholes that still remain intact.

Shackleton, one of history's most celebrated Antarctic explorers, died on Quest in 1922 at age 47. He suffered a heart attack while the ship was anchored in South Georgia, a remote island in the South Atlantic. 

'SPECTACULAR' SHIPWRECK FOUND WITH UNDERWATER TIME CAPSULE OF UNTOUCHED CARGO: 'AMAZING FIND'

After his death, Quest was later sold to Norwegian owners. It spent decades sailing in Arctic waters before being crushed by ice floes and sinking in the Labrador Sea in 1962.

John Geiger, CEO of the RCGS, described seeing Quest for the first time as "a moving experience."

"To see Shackleton's ship, and to think that Shackleton was standing on that deck a century ago... At first, there was a lot of darkness, but suddenly the bow emerges as you are going toward it. It's incredible," Geiger said in a press release.

UNDERWATER ROBOTICS EXPERT REVEALS 'SHIPWRECK CITY' HIDING BENEATH MAJOR URBAN LAKE

The team used WHOI's Falcon ROV to image the ship and create its digital twin, as well as DSV Alvin, the iconic submersible that first visited the Titanic wreck 40 years ago. The vessels were made available through the National Science Foundation.

Coleman of WHOI, who is based in Rhode Island, said a major part of his job was creating a digital twin of the shipwreck.

The ocean scientist said he was surprised to find the wreck covered in fishing nets and teeming with marine life.

"I wasn't expecting all the fishing gear, the nets and all the fish," he said. "I was honestly thinking it was a little bit deeper and in cold water, and that it would be pretty well-preserved and free of fishing gear because I didn't think there was that much fishing up there."

CENTURIES-OLD PIRATE MYSTERY DEEPENS AFTER WRECKS ARE FOUND NEAR BAHAMAS HAVEN

Added Coleman, "Boy, was I wrong. … It was a vibrant sort of marine life ecosystem around it."

While much of the ship remains recognizable, Coleman said its wooden components are "rapidly deteriorating" after decades in the underwater environment.

"A lot of the wood was collapsing and degrading. The wooden deck was basically completely gone," he said.

"The metal structures of the ship were still pretty well intact, although deteriorating."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Coleman said researchers hope to preserve the wreck through detailed digital mapping rather than artifact recovery.

"We understand most of the components that we could find on it, so you're not really learning anything about history by recovering the artifacts. … There really isn't much need to," he said.

Expeditions like this help researchers better understand both maritime history and the marine ecosystems around historic shipwrecks, he added.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"By studying them, we can bring recognition to history and oceanography," Coleman said. "These shipwrecks are now artificial reefs that support diverse sorts of biological communities."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

He added, "We care about those communities. We want to understand how animals live in the deep ocean. So, by bringing this project to the public, the public can gain a deeper appreciation for history and for the ocean."

The newly released images come not long after another Shackleton-linked discovery garnered international attention.

In October 2025, researchers challenged the long-held belief that Shackleton's famed expedition ship Endurance sank solely because it was crushed by Antarctic ice. They argued instead that structural flaws in the vessel also contributed to its loss.
