item.title: Departure of New York Times columnist puts a spotlight on the void of pro-Trump voices in its opinion pages
item.description: Ross Douthat's departure to CBS leaves The New York Times with 12 opinion columnists, only two of whom identify as conservative — and were both Kamala Harris voters.
item.content:encoded:
The paper of record doesn't have a representative for roughly half of the U.S. voting population — at least on its opinion pages.

The New York Times has 12 featured columnists following the departure of its longtime conservative writer Ross Douthat, who was poached by CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss last week as a new "60 Minutes" correspondent.

According to a drop-down menu on the Times' homepage, the remaining columnists are Jamelle Bouie, Maureen Dowd, David French, Thomas Friedman, M. Gessen, Michelle Goldberg, Ezra Klein, Nicholas Kristof, Carlos Lozada, Tressie McMillan Cottom, Lydia Polgreen and Bret Stephens.

NYT COLUMNIST SAYS SHE 'DEEPLY' REGRETS PRAISING SENATE HOPEFUL AFTER RAPE ALLEGATION

Of the Times' 12 columnists, only two of them, David French and Bret Stephens, are self-described conservatives but have spent the past decade opposing President Donald Trump, so much so that they both declared their support for Kamala Harris in the 2024 election.

Douthat's new boss, notably, was formerly a Times colleague of his. Weiss resigned from the Gray Lady as an opinion editor in 2020 after being ostracized and bullied by far-left staffers, famously declaring at the time that "Twitter has become [the Times'] ultimate editor." 

Her resignation followed the debacle at the paper after publishing the now-infamous Tom Cotton op-ed in 2020 about using federal troops to quell civil unrest. That prompted a volcanic social media revolt from liberal Times employees and the ousting of multiple opinion staffers in one of the most embarrassing episodes in the paper's recent history.

NYT COLUMNIST 'TORN' ABOUT ROOTING FOR IRANIAN REGIME'S DOWNFALL SINCE IT WOULD GIVE A WIN TO TRUMP, NETANYAHU

The politics of the remaining Times columnists can be seen in their recent commentary and the controversies they've been swept up in. In April, Thomas Friedman said he found himself "torn" about rooting for the Iranian regime's downfall if it meant it would be a victory for "terrible," "awful human beings" President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

In May, Nicholas Kristof sparked an international outcry when he reported without skepticism that Palestinian prisoners detained in Israel were being raped by dogs — Kristof also made an ill-fated bid for Oregon governor in 2021, as a Democrat. 

Last month, Goldberg was forced to walk back her fawning coverage of disgraced Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner after the Democrat was accused of sexual assault.

ISRAELI PM NETANYAHU INITIATING DEFAMATION LAWSUIT AGAINST NEW YORK TIMES OVER CONTROVERSIAL ‘DOG RAPE’ STORY

The overwhelming liberal slant of the Times' opinion pages can also apply to the paper's editorial board, which hasn't endorsed a Republican for president since Dwight D. Eisenhower nearly 70 years ago. In 17 straight elections, it's endorsed the Democratic candidate, including defeated hopefuls like George McGovern, Walter Mondale, Michael Dukakis, John Kerry, Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris.

Just two days after Trump won the 2024 election, The New York Times published a somber video featuring 10 of its columnists, including Douthat, French and Stephens, all offering their predictions of "the worst version of a Trump administration."

In the video, Polgreen insisted Trump will "fulfill his promise to be a dictator on Day One."

Meanwhile, the opinion pages at The Washington Post have had quite the makeover. Its owner, Jeff Bezos, quashed its planned endorsement of Harris and implemented an edict for its opinion section to promote "personal liberties and free markets," prompting major backlash from liberal critics.

"Our readers are overwhelmingly liberal, right?" Washington Post opinion editor Adam O'Neal told Fox News Digital last year, who announced last week he is leaving The Post at the end of August. "And they're all overwhelmingly located in blue states. And just a few blue states. And they're over-represented on the coasts. And so, one way to look at it would be to say, 'Well, if you're non-partisan, and you have a highly partisan readership, they may be offended by that.' And maybe that's true. But looking forward as I rebuild, I really just see it as an opportunity to expand our reach."

But with Douthat's departure from the Times, the conservative representation in its opinion pages becomes even smaller — and what little remains is fervently anti-Trump.

The New York Times did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

item.title: Steelers defend Aaron Rodgers' right to voice opinions after ESPN Fauci segment
item.description: The Pittsburgh Steelers defended Aaron Rodgers' right to voice his opinion after his ESPN segment about Anthony Fauci sparked social media backlash.
item.content:encoded:
The Aaron Rodgers segment on ESPN got folks on both sides of the Anthony Fauci debate quite riled up on Monday.

People got angry at ESPN — some for allowing Rodgers on air at all, and others because he was steered away from discussing the Dianna Russini and Mike Vrabel scandal on air.

Some people defended Rodgers for calling out Fauci for pleading the Fifth Amendment 111 times during recent U.S. Senate hearings.

AARON RODGERS EVISCERATES ANTHONY FAUCI AFTER PLEADING THE FIFTH AT SENATE HEARING: 'ABSOLUTE CRIMINAL'

And others attacked Rodgers for lying about his COVID-19 vaccine status or otherwise just not agreeing with their viewpoint.

The segment on "The Pat McAfee Show" left no safe space for anyone, including the "progrum" itself.

The issue became so fiery on social media that the Pittsburgh Steelers felt the need to address the situation.

So, the club is defending Rodgers and his right to voice his opinion.

"Discussions around culture and politics can bring differing perspectives, and our players are entitled to their own personal views," Steelers spokesman Burt Lauten said in a statement to Fox News Digital/OutKick.

"With respect to that, I am certain there are a variety of opinions on many topics within our locker room."

It appears the Steelers believe that people, including their players, have a right to their own opinions.

Imagine that. It's as if the Steelers are located in America and have read the U.S. Constitution.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Chalk one up for freedom of expression. And chalk one up for the Steelers, which have been notably consistent in this manner in the past.

You'll recall in May 2025, Mason Rudolph, another Steelers quarterback, incited online approval as well as backlash for having the nerve to appear with Vietnam War veteran and former Steelers running back Rocky Bleier and President Donald Trump at a rally at the U.S. Steel's Irvin Works plant in West Mifflin, Pennsylvania.

Trump welcomed Rudolph on stage and predicted big things for the player, saying, "He's going to be the guy."

Fans went nuts.

MAGA immediately rallied to Rudolph and bought more jerseys than any backup quarterback has a right to sell.

Socialists, Democrats, liberals, progressives, communists, including the Viet Cong, people who hate puppies, anarchists, and perhaps Iran (kidding) despised the moment as an utter betrayal of the Steelers' six Super Bowl titles and the Terrible Towel.

The Steelers themselves, meanwhile, reacted with aplomb. With sanity. With class.

"Our alumni and current players make their own individual decisions and these do not necessarily reflect the views of the Pittsburgh Steelers organization," the club said in an email to fans who complained.

And now, with this Rodgers appearance, the club is sticking to its practice of acknowledging viral public reaction, defending its players' right to an opinion, and not really taking a side.

This is more than good public relations. It's public good policy.

The Steelers recognize that their locker room is a melting pot of races, religions, ideas, and opinions. And no one representing any one cause is more respected or heard than anyone else by the organization.

Rodgers undoubtedly has the team's loudest megaphone. And he uses it quite deftly to relay his opinions. So it would be counterproductive for the Steelers to in any way kneecap that or him.

So, the club is going to do what is best for club peace – which in this case comes with the added advantage of being the right thing to do.

item.title: WWE star Brie Bella says she'll be 'out for a bit' after suffering broken scapula during SummerSlam match
item.description: Brie Bella revealed she broke her scapula during her SummerSlam six-woman tag team match but somehow finished the bout before heading to the hospital.
item.content:encoded:
WWE star Brie Bella announced Monday she will be "out for a bit" after suffering a broken scapula during her six-woman tag team match at SummerSlam over the weekend.

Bella made the revelation in a post on her Instagram account and thanked fans for their outpouring of support.

"I wanted to thank you all for sending me all the love, warm wishes and prayers," she wrote. "When I was sitting in the hospital, I was reading everything you guys were sending my way, love you all!!! Unfortunately I’ll be out for a bit. I broke my scapula. If there’s one thing I know about my sister and I is that we don’t let broken bones stop us. Not sure how I finished that match, but I do believe between the adrenaline, passion for the business and the love for all the women I work with, it gave me the drive to finish.

"Now my new journey starts!! Buddy said he’s going to be my assistant, Birdie‘s going to be my nurse and they both told me that daddy is going to be my personal chef, so I am set!! if there is one thing I know about Brie Mode, she always finds a way to come back to her wrestling home. Let the recovery begin."

Bella appeared to suffer the injury after taking a move from opponent Jacy Jayne. Bella was seated next to the steel steps when her opponent, Jacy Jayne, hit a running senton on her. At that moment, she began to clutch her shoulder and kept rubbing it during the rest of the match with her sister Nikki Bella and Paige.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

WWE Chief Content Officer Paul "Triple H" Levesque told reporters after Night 1 that the injury "seems pretty bad."

"Yeah, she’s injured," he said. "I don’t have an update yet. We’ve taken her. She was here, got some treatment done here, has been taken to the hospital to get some scans done. Don’t have a clean answer on it yet.

"I know she hurt her shoulder. It seems pretty bad, but I don’t have an answer yet. Hopefully we will soon. Hopefully, it won’t be as bad as we thought it was, but that’s the nature of the game."

The Bellas and Paige teamed up against Jayne, Lainey Reid and Fallon Henley. Jayne scored the pinfall over Paige to give her team the win.

Brie Bella made her stunning return to WWE at the Royal Rumble in January and then was set to team with her sister at WrestleMania 42 before Nikki Bella suffered her own injury.

Instead, she teamed with Paige as they won the WWE Women’s Tag Team Championship.

Now, Brie will be on the shelf for the time being while Nikki eyes singles gold.
